title: Retentive Network: A Successor to Transformer for LLMs

pages.title: The impossible triangle
pages.subtitle: Why you couldn't have fast training AND fast inference AND good quality — until now

blocks.html: Every architecture that runs large language models has been forced to give up one of three things. The Transformer trains fast (it processes a whole sequence at once on the GPU) and is accurate, but its inference is expensive: to generate token number 1,000 it must re-attend to all 999 previous tokens, so cost grows with sequence length and a giant KV cache piles up in memory. Older RNNs invert the trade-off: generating a token is cheap (just update one hidden state), but you cannot train them in parallel and quality lags. Linear-attention tricks speed up inference but historically lose accuracy.

The paper names this the "impossible triangle" (Figure 2): the three corners are training parallelism, low-cost (O(1)) inference, and strong performance. Before RetNet, you could reach at most two corners at once. Retentive Network (RetNet) is the claim that you can hit all three.
In this work, we propose Retentive Network (RetNet) as a foundation architecture for large language models, simultaneously achieving training parallelism, low-cost inference, and good performance.

The trick is one mechanism — retention — that has three mathematically equivalent forms. You compute the same function whichever way you run it. Use the parallel form during training (full GPU utilization, like a Transformer). Use the recurrent form during inference (update a fixed-size state per token, O(1) cost, no growing KV cache). Use the chunkwise recurrent form for very long sequences (parallel inside each chunk, recurrent across chunks). Same weights, same outputs, three runtimes.

An analogy: think of a sum like $1+2+3+\\dots+n$. You can add all the terms at once on paper (parallel), or keep a running total and add one number at a time (recurrent), or split into blocks, sum each block in parallel, then carry block-totals forward (chunkwise). All give the same answer; you pick the method that fits the situation. Retention does this for sequence modeling.

Headline numbers from the abstract and experiments: compared to Transformers at 7B parameters with 8k-length sequences, RetNet decodes 8.4x faster, uses 70% less memory during inference, its inference latency is length-invariant (flat as the sequence grows), and training is 25–50% faster with less GPU memory — all while matching or beating Transformer language-modeling quality once models pass roughly 2B parameters.

pages.title: From attention to retention
pages.subtitle: Replace softmax with a decay term you can unroll as a recurrence

blocks.html: The whole paper hinges on one observation: if you remove softmax from attention, the computation becomes a recurrence you can also run in parallel. Softmax is what forces a Transformer to materialize the full $n \\times n$ attention matrix and re-read the past at every step. Retention swaps the softmax for a simple exponential decay by position, and that single change is what unlocks all three forms.

Imagine a state $s_n$ that summarizes everything seen up to position $n$. At each step you decay the old state a little and add the new token's contribution, then read out an answer. Concretely the paper begins from a state-space recurrence mapping input $x_n$ to output $o_n$ through state $s_n$:

blocks.tex: s_n = A s_{n-1} + K_n^{\\top} v_n, \\qquad o_n = Q_n s_n = \\sum_{m=1}^{n} Q_n A^{\\,n-m} K_m^{\\top} v_m

blocks.html: Reading it term by term: $s_n \\in \\mathbb{R}^{d \\times d}$ is the running state (a small matrix, not a growing cache). $A \\in \\mathbb{R}^{d \\times d}$ is a transition matrix that decays the old state. $v_n$ is the value vector for token $n$, and $K_n, Q_n$ are its key and query (row vectors of dimension $d$), exactly as in attention. $o_n$ is the output at position $n$. The second equality just unrolls the recurrence: the contribution of an earlier token $m$ is weighted by $A^{\\,n-m}$, i.e. how many steps ago it occurred — that is the decay.

The authors then make $A$ a diagonalizable matrix, $A = \\Lambda(\\gamma e^{i\\theta})\\Lambda^{-1}$. Folding the change-of-basis $\\Lambda$ into the learnable $Q$ and $K$ projections, the power $A^{\\,n-m}$ becomes $\\gamma^{\\,n-m} e^{i(n-m)\\theta}$. The output becomes:

Here $\\gamma \\in (0,1)$ is a real decay rate — a scalar that says how fast the past fades (smaller $\\gamma$ = shorter memory). The factor $e^{i\\theta}$ rotates by an angle proportional to relative distance $n-m$; this is exactly the xPos / rotary-style relative position encoding, now baked directly into retention rather than added on. So $(\\gamma e^{i\\theta})^{\\,n-m}$ does two jobs at once: a magnitude $\\gamma^{\\,n-m}$ that decays with distance, and a phase that encodes position.

Why it works: softmax gave attention two properties — a normalized weighting and the ability to look anywhere in the past. Retention keeps "look anywhere" but replaces the normalized softmax weighting with a fixed, position-only decay $\\gamma^{\\,n-m}$. Because that decay is just a power of a constant, the sum telescopes into a recurrence — which softmax could never do, since each softmax weight depends on all the other scores at once. Giving up data-dependent normalization is the price; O(1) inference is what you buy.

pages.title: The parallel form: train like a Transformer
pages.subtitle: Same matrix-multiply shape as attention, with a decay mask instead of softmax

blocks.html: During training you want to use the whole GPU, processing all $n$ positions simultaneously. The recurrence above is sequential, so the paper rewrites the exact same function as a batched matrix product — the parallel representation. This is what makes RetNet trainable at Transformer speed.
First project the input $X \\in \\mathbb{R}^{|x| \\times d_{model}}$ into queries, keys, and values, then form the output:

Term by term: $W_Q, W_K, W_V \\in \\mathbb{R}^{d \\times d}$ are the learned projection matrices. $\\Theta_n = e^{i n \\theta}$ is the per-position phase (the rotary part); $\\overline{\\Theta}$ is its complex conjugate, and $\\odot$ is elementwise multiplication. $Q K^{\\top} \\in \\mathbb{R}^{n \\times n}$ is the familiar query-key score matrix — identical in shape to attention. The new ingredient is $D \\in \\mathbb{R}^{n \\times n}$, the decay mask, which replaces softmax.

$D_{nm}$ is the weight that position $n$ (the query) puts on position $m$ (the key). It does two things in one stroke: the lower-triangular structure ($0$ when $ncausal mask — you can't attend to the future — and the value $\\gamma^{\\,n-m}$ is the distance decay. A token 3 steps back gets weight $\\gamma^3$; one 100 steps back gets $\\gamma^{100}$, which is tiny. There is no row normalization — unlike softmax, the weights are fixed by position alone.

Concrete mini-example. Take $\\gamma = 0.9$ and look at the query at position $n=4$. Its decay weights over keys $m = 1,2,3,4$ are $\\gamma^3, \\gamma^2, \\gamma^1, \\gamma^0 = 0.729,\\ 0.81,\\ 0.9,\\ 1.0$. The most recent token (distance 0) gets full weight 1; older tokens fade geometrically. Multiply these into the row of $QK^{\\top}$, sum, and you have $o_4$ — the same number the recurrence would have produced, but computed in one matrix multiply alongside every other position.

Why this is the key move: the parallel form has the exact computational shape of attention ($O(n^2)$ matmuls, fully parallel, GPU-friendly), so training cost and code barely change. But because $D$ is a pure power-of-$\\gamma$ mask rather than a softmax, the very same computation can be re-expressed as a recurrence for inference. One function, two faces.

pages.title: The recurrent & chunkwise forms
pages.subtitle: O(1) decoding, plus a hybrid for very long sequences

blocks.html: Training in parallel is half the win. The payoff comes at inference: the recurrent representation turns generation into a fixed-cost state update, with no KV cache and no dependence on sequence length.

blocks.tex: S_n = \\gamma\\, S_{n-1} + K_n^{\\top} V_n, \\qquad \\text{Retention}(X_n) = Q_n S_n

blocks.html: Reading it: $S_n \\in \\mathbb{R}^{d \\times d}$ is the running state — a fixed-size $d \\times d$ matrix that does not grow with the sequence. At each new token you scale the old state by the decay $\\gamma$, add the outer product $K_n^{\\top} V_n$ of the new token's key and value, then read out $o_n = Q_n S_n$. That is it. Generating token 10,000 costs exactly the same as generating token 10 — constant time, constant memory. Contrast a Transformer, whose KV cache holds all 9,999 previous keys/values and whose attention re-scans them every step.

This is the same function as the parallel form — unrolling $S_n = \\gamma S_{n-1} + K_n^{\\top} V_n$ gives $o_n = \\sum_{m \\le n} \\gamma^{\\,n-m} Q_n K_m^{\\top} V_m$, which is exactly row $n$ of $(QK^{\\top} \\odot D)V$. The two representations are provably identical; the paper just runs whichever is cheaper for the task.

blocks.text: Chunkwise form: the best of both

blocks.html: For training or prefilling on very long sequences, the pure parallel form's $O(n^2)$ memory is wasteful and the pure recurrent form is too sequential. The chunkwise recurrent form splits the sequence into blocks of length $B$: inside each block use the parallel form; across blocks carry a state forward recurrently.

Here $[i]$ indexes the $i$-th chunk, $R_i \\in \\mathbb{R}^{d \\times d}$ is the cross-chunk state passed between blocks (scaled by $\\gamma^{B}$, the decay accumulated over a full block of length $B$), and $\\zeta, \\xi$ are within-chunk decay factors that line up positions correctly. The first term handles interactions within the chunk in parallel; the second injects everything from before the chunk via the single state $R_{i-1}$. Complexity drops to $O(n B + B^2)$ — linear in $n$ for fixed chunk size — which is why RetNet can scale to long sequences with a flat memory footprint.

items: Parallel form → training: maximal GPU use, O(n²), same as a Transformer.
Recurrent form → autoregressive decoding: O(1) per token, fixed state, no KV cache.
Chunkwise form → long-sequence training / prefill: O(n) memory, parallel inside chunks, recurrent across them.

pages.title: Multi-scale retention & the full block
pages.subtitle: Different heads remember at different timescales

blocks.html: A single decay rate $\\gamma$ is a blunt instrument: too small and the model forgets long-range context; too large and recent tokens don't stand out. RetNet's fix is multi-scale retention (MSR) — like multi-head attention, but each head is assigned its own decay $\\gamma$, so different heads specialize in different memory horizons.

Concretely, with $h$ heads the decays are spread geometrically across the range, e.g. $\\gamma = 1 - 2^{-5-\\text{arange}(0,h)}$. The paper's intuition: some heads get a $\\gamma$ near 1 (long memory, they track the gist of the whole document) while others get a smaller $\\gamma$ (short memory, they sharpen local detail). The decays are fixed, not learned, which keeps training stable and means the rates need no tuning.

Each $\\text{head}_i$ runs the retention computation with its own decay $\\gamma_i$. The heads are concatenated, normalized by a GroupNorm (one group per head), then mixed by the output projection $W_O \\in \\mathbb{R}^{d \\times d}$. The per-head GroupNorm matters because heads with different $\\gamma$ produce outputs at very different scales (a long-memory head sums many terms); normalizing each head independently keeps them comparable and stabilizes training. The paper also adds a swish gate to the block before $W_O$.
The full RetNet layer then looks exactly like a Transformer layer with one substitution — MSR in place of self-attention:

$X^l$ is the input to layer $l$, $\\text{LN}$ is LayerNorm, $\\text{FFN}(X) = \\text{gelu}(XW_1)W_2$ is the same position-wise feed-forward network a Transformer uses, and the two $+\\,X$ terms are residual connections. Everything outside the attention sublayer is unchanged — same FFN, residuals, and norms — which is deliberate: it lets RetNet reuse Transformer training recipes and makes the comparison apples-to-apples.

Trivia: the fixed multi-scale decays echo earlier ideas (ALiBi's per-head linear biases, the gating in linear-attention works like RWKV), but RetNet is the first to package them so that the same mechanism is provably parallel, recurrent, and chunkwise at once.

pages.title: Quality, speed, and memory
pages.subtitle: The numbers behind the impossible-triangle claim

blocks.html: An architecture that is fast but worse isn't a successor — it's a niche. So the central question for the experiments is: does RetNet actually match Transformer quality while delivering the efficiency? The answer the paper reports is yes, with a clear crossover point in model size.

Training models from 1.3B to 6.7B parameters on a 100B-token corpus, RetNet's validation perplexity tracks the Transformer's and crosses over to be consistently better above roughly 2B parameters (Figure 5 / the scaling curves). At 6.7B, in-context learning (zero-/few-shot on downstream tasks) is on par with or above the size-matched Transformer.
The paper's takeaway is that RetNet is a strong scaling law: the bigger the model, the more it favors RetNet over the Transformer — exactly the regime that matters for LLMs.

items: Decoding throughput: ~8.4x higher than a 7B Transformer at 8k sequence length, and RetNet's throughput stays roughly flat as batch/length grow while the Transformer's collapses.
Memory: ~3.4x lower GPU memory during inference (about 70% less) — there is no KV cache, just the fixed d×d state.
Latency: length-invariant. Per-token latency barely moves from short to long sequences, whereas Transformer latency climbs with context length and batch size.
Training: 25–50% memory saving and ~7x speedup over a standard Transformer baseline when using chunkwise retention with FlashAttention-style kernels.

blocks.html: Why these gains are structural, not incidental: they fall straight out of the recurrent form. No KV cache means inference memory is $O(1)$ in length instead of $O(n)$; constant per-token work means latency doesn't grow with context. A Transformer cannot get these without changing its math — which is precisely RetNet's pitch.

The paper ablates the design choices and finds each earns its place: removing the multi-scale decay (using a single $\\gamma$) hurts perplexity; removing the per-head GroupNorm destabilizes training; the swish gate and the chosen head dimension both help. The decays themselves are not learned, confirming that fixed multi-scale rates are enough.

pages.title: Why RetNet matters
pages.subtitle: A genuine alternative to attention, and where it sits in the field

blocks.html: RetNet's contribution is conceptual as much as empirical: it shows that the parallel-training / recurrent-inference duality — long thought to force a choice — can be one mechanism. That reframes the design space. The famous "Attention is All You Need" made parallel training the default; RetNet argues that for generation, the recurrent view is what you actually want, and you can have both.

This places RetNet in the lineage of efficient-attention and linear-attention work (Linear Transformers, Performer, RWKV, S4/state-space models) but distinguishes it by hitting all three triangle corners at once where prior methods sacrificed quality or parallelism. It is a direct intellectual sibling of state-space models like Mamba that arrived around the same time — both reach for a recurrence you can also parallelize.

Practical impact: the O(1) decoder and absent KV cache are exactly the bottlenecks that make long-context LLM serving expensive. RetNet's flat latency and 70%-lower inference memory point at cheaper, longer-context deployment — the same Microsoft Research group (which also produced BitNet and the Differential Transformer) was explicitly hunting for a more deployable foundation architecture.

The honest caveats. The fixed exponential decay gives every head a hard recency bias — there is no data-dependent way to "jump back" to an arbitrary far token the way softmax attention can, which can matter for tasks needing precise long-range recall. And the quality crossover only appears above ~2B parameters; at small scale a Transformer can still win. RetNet is best read not as a finished replacement but as a serious proof that the impossible triangle was never actually impossible.

RetNet achieves low-cost inference, efficient long-sequence modeling, Transformer-comparable performance, and parallel model training simultaneously. ... These intriguing properties make RetNet a strong successor to Transformer for large language models.
